criteria.rationale: Verified: dispatch passes the run's sealed-checkout path to the adapter environment, Linux excludes its own PID, and abandoned release requires a dead owner. Unresolved: /proc visibility and PID identity can change between inspection and signal, and the reservation precedes marker publication (N1, N3, N4). Accepted spec limits: a process that clears the marker escapes (L1), and non-Linux cleanup remains process-group-only (L2); the manual's omission of L2 is N5.
The release writes the existing version-1 ReviewRun and attempt-receipt formats; earlier records retain their parser and meaning. I checked the run ledger and delegate list projections.

D1 addresses the observed session-escape cause by finding processes with the run-specific sealed-checkout entry and doing so after adapter/group termination but before cleanup inventory. D2 uses the existing failed-run and receipt records so older readers retain ordinary failed-run semantics. The design assessment reports no structural deltas; N1, N3, and N4 identify conditions where this design does not complete its promised lifecycle.
I compared the root and scaffold manuals in both locales with the Linux and non-Linux implementations and the spec's L2 limit.
The change stays within the stated dispatcher, attempt ledger, brief and manual scope; the design assessment found no structural deltas.

Process-group-only cleanup is the smallest change but misses commands in their own sessions, so D1's per-run marker scan is a proportionate extension. D2 reuses the existing failed-run and receipt contract rather than adding a new ledger schema. The negative space is explicit: cleared markers and non-Linux platforms remain outside the guarantee (L1/L2); procfs denial and PID reuse are concrete invalidation conditions recorded as N3/N4.

findings.action: The reservation is published before the active marker. A dispatch stopped in that gap leaves a reservation with no run or marker, so delegate ls cannot expose it and later admission remains blocked.
A stalled attempt is listed with only its state and timestamp; the abandonment cause required by R5 is omitted from both text and JSON projections.

The process is identified by numeric PID and later signaled by PID without pinning process identity; if it exits and the PID is reused between inspection and SIGKILL, an unrelated process can be killed.

The /proc scan treats ReadDir failure as an empty process set, skips unreadable environ files, and treats stat read failures as process exit; a leftover can survive while the dispatcher reports successful reaping and proceeds to cleanup.
The manual claims environment-marked process reaping without limiting the claim to Linux; review_reap_other.go is a no-op and the spec records process-group-only cleanup on other platforms.
